subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive the expression for the intensity at a point where interference of light occurs. Arrive at the conditions for maximum and zero intensity.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked line by line: y₁ + y₂ with the R cos α / R sin α substitution gives y = R sin(ωt + α); squaring and adding gives R² = 2a²(1 + cos φ) = 4a² cos²(φ/2); I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2); maxima at φ = 2nπ (δ = nλ) with I = 4I₀; minima at φ = (2n+1)π (δ = (2n+1)λ/2) with I = 0. The book's printed equation (2) has a typo — it ends in a cos ωt cos φ where the line above it correctly derives a cos ωt sin φ; the derivation here uses the correct sin φ term. NOTE FOR THE FOUNDER: this SAQ is LAQ-grade content (a full derivation plus both conditions) but the book prints it under Short Answer Questions and this chapter has no LAQ section, so it stays a 4-mark SAQ.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: This 4-mark question is a full derivation — know every algebra line, not just I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2), because the middle lines are where the marks sit.

steps.label: The two-source arrangement
steps.margin_note: No separate mark for the figure here, but it fixes every symbol: slits S₁ S₂ a distance d apart, screen at distance D, P at height x above the centre O.
steps.why: Every symbol in the derivation is defined by this picture — d, D, x, P and the two paths whose difference is δ. Drawing it first means no symbol arrives unexplained.
common_mistakes: Marking d from a slit to the screen. d is the separation of the two slits; D is the slit-to-screen distance.

recall.must_convey: That two slits S₁ and S₂, a distance d apart, send waves to a point P on a screen at distance D, at height x above the centre O.
accept: draw the two slits and the screen

steps.memory_tip: Three lengths in the picture: d between the slits, D to the screen, x up the screen.

steps.label: Resultant displacement
lines: S₁ and S₂ are two coherent sources: same
wavelength λ, same amplitude a, in phase.
At a point P on the screen the two waves
arrive with a phase difference φ.
The path difference δ gives φ = (2π/λ) δ.

lines.text: y₁ = a sin ωt ;  y₂ = a sin (ωt + φ)

lines: The resultant displacement is y = y₁ + y₂

lines.text: y = a sin ωt (1 + cos φ) + a cos ωt sin φ

lines: Put a(1 + cos φ) = R cos α and

lines.text: a sin φ = R sin α

steps.margin_note: First mark. Expand sin(ωt + φ), group the sin ωt and cos ωt terms, then substitute R cos α and R sin α.
steps.why: The whole derivation is one idea: two sine waves of the same frequency add to a single sine wave of the same frequency with a new amplitude R. The R cos α / R sin α substitution is what turns the two-term sum into that single sine wave.
common_mistakes: Writing the second term as a cos ωt cos φ. Expanding a sin(ωt + φ) gives a cos ωt sin φ — the printed book has this typo in its equation (2).
Giving the two waves different amplitudes. This derivation takes equal amplitudes a; that is what later makes the minima exactly zero.

recall.must_convey: That the two displacements a sin ωt and a sin(ωt + φ) add, and the substitution R cos α, R sin α turns the sum into y = R sin(ωt + α).
accept: R cos alpha and R sin alpha substitution
y is R sine omega t plus alpha

steps.memory_tip: Two sine waves, one frequency — the sum is again a sine wave; only the amplitude is new.

steps.label: Resultant amplitude
lines: Squaring and adding the two substitutions:

lines.text: R² = a²(1 + cos φ)² + a² sin²φ
R² = a²(1 + 2 cos φ + cos²φ + sin²φ)

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Square both substitutions, add, use sin²α + cos²α = 1, then the half-angle identity.
steps.why: Squaring and adding removes α, which was only a helper angle: cos²α + sin²α = 1 on the left leaves R² alone. The half-angle identity 1 + cos φ = 2 cos²(φ/2) is what produces the clean cos²(φ/2) the conditions are read from.
common_mistakes: Stopping at R² = 2a²(1 + cos φ) without the half-angle step — the conditions for maxima and minima need the cos²(φ/2) form.
Losing the cross term 2 cos φ when expanding (1 + cos φ)².

recall.must_convey: That squaring and adding the substitutions gives R² = 2a²(1 + cos φ), which the half-angle identity turns into R = 2a cos(φ/2).
accept: square and add to remove alpha
one plus cos phi is two cos squared phi by two
reject: intensity is proportional to amplitude squared

steps.memory_tip: Square and add removes α; the half-angle identity gives cos(φ/2).

steps.label: Intensity expression
lines: Intensity is proportional to the square of
If I₀ is the intensity due to one source
steps.margin_note: Third mark. State I ∝ R², name I₀ as the single-source intensity, and box the result.
steps.why: Intensity, not displacement, is what the eye and the screen record, and intensity goes as the amplitude squared. Writing I₀ for the one-source intensity turns 4a² cos²(φ/2) into the standard form 4I₀ cos²(φ/2).
common_mistakes: Writing I = 2I₀ cos²(φ/2). The peak of the pattern is four times one source, not two — the factor comes from R = 2a.
Treating I₀ as the total incident intensity. I₀ is the intensity each source would give alone.

recall.must_convey: That intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so with I₀ the one-source intensity, I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2).
accept: four I nought cos squared phi by two
I nought is one source alone
reject: maximum at phi equal to 2 n pi

steps.memory_tip: Amplitude doubles at best (2a), so intensity at best is 4 times one source.

steps.label: Maximum and zero intensity
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Each condition in BOTH languages — phase difference and path difference — with the intensity value it gives.
steps.why: The conditions are read straight off cos²(φ/2): it is 1 when φ/2 is a multiple of π and 0 when φ/2 is an odd multiple of π/2. Translating each φ into a path difference through δ = (φ/2π)λ gives the nλ and (2n+1)λ/2 forms the examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two conditions — whole-wavelength path difference is BRIGHT, odd half-wavelength is DARK.
Giving only the phase form. State the path-difference form as well: δ = nλ for maxima, (2n+1)λ/2 for minima.
Writing the minimum intensity as small but not zero. With equal amplitudes the dark bands are exactly zero.

recall.must_convey: That maxima occur at φ = 2nπ, path difference nλ, with I = 4I₀; minima at φ = (2n+1)π, path difference (2n+1)λ/2, with I = 0.
accept: maxima at path difference n lambda
minima at odd multiples of half wavelength
four I nought maximum and zero minimum

steps.memory_tip: Whole wavelengths agree — bright. Half wavelengths oppose — dark.
